faq.heading: Frequently asked
faq.tagline: Short answers to the big questions people ask about size and space.
faq.q1: What is the smallest thing in the universe?
faq.a1: The smallest things we have measured — quarks and electrons — behave like points: no size has been detected down to about 10⁻¹⁸ m. Far below that, the Planck length (1.6 × 10⁻³⁵ m) marks where our best theories stop working. Whether anything smaller can exist is still unknown.
faq.q2: What is the largest known star?
faq.a2: Red supergiants and hypergiants such as UY Scuti and Stephenson 2-18 are among the largest stars known by radius — placed where the Sun is, UY Scuti's surface would reach past Mars, and the very largest might extend beyond Jupiter. They are also among the shortest-lived stars in the galaxy.
faq.q3: What is the largest known black hole?
faq.a3: TON 618 and Phoenix-A are leading candidates for the most massive known black holes, each weighing tens of billions of solar masses — roughly ten thousand times more than the supermassive black hole at the centre of our Milky Way (Sagittarius A*).
faq.q4: How far is the observable universe?
faq.a4: The cosmic horizon is roughly 46 billion light-years from Earth in every direction, making the full observable universe a sphere about 93 billion light-years across. Beyond it almost certainly lies more space we can never see.
faq.a5: An invisible form of matter whose gravity holds galaxies together. It outweighs ordinary matter about five to one. We map it through gravitational lensing, but its particle nature is still unknown.
faq.a6: A still-unexplained energy that appears to be accelerating the expansion of the universe. It accounts for roughly 68% of the total mass-energy of the cosmos.
faq.a7: Not as far as anyone knows. Einstein's equations allow wormholes, but none has ever been observed, and keeping one open would need 'exotic matter' with negative energy that has never been found in usable amounts. They remain speculative — a fascinating possibility, not a discovery.
faq.q8: How long would it take to reach the nearest star?
faq.a8: Proxima Centauri is 4.24 light-years away, so light takes 4.24 years. Voyager 1, travelling at about 61,000 km/h, would need roughly 75,000 years; even Parker Solar Probe at its record 690,000 km/h would take about 6,650 years.

categories.COSMOS.description: Galaxies, stars, neutron-dense corpses, and the dark side of the universe — the largest scales we can observe.
categories.MICRO_WORLD.description: Quarks, atoms, and molecules — the building blocks underneath everything you can see or touch.
categories.HUMAN_MIND.description: Documented oddities of how a single brain — and a single body — can house more than one self.
categories.ANCIENT_HISTORY.description: Monuments and mysteries whose construction still resists complete explanation.
categories.COSMOS.intro: The universe at every scale beyond the ground beneath your feet — planets, stars, galaxies, and the largest gravitationally bound structures we know how to find. More than half of the stops on Quantumaire live here, because the cosmos is where orders of magnitude start to do real work. The Cosmos category also collects the abstractions that hold it all together: dark matter, dark energy, the cosmic horizon.
categories.MICRO_WORLD.intro: Everything smaller than the cell. Quarks and gluons inside the proton; the proton inside the atom; the atom inside the DNA helix; the helix inside the virus; the virus, in turn, dwarfed by a bacterium. Each step down this ladder is roughly a thousand times smaller than the last, so the human-scale intuition that 'small things differ by a bit' breaks completely. The micro-world is where you watch that intuition snap.
categories.HUMAN_MIND.intro: Phenomena that don't fit on the size axis at all because they're properties of the brain rather than measurable objects. Quantumaire includes one such stop — dissociative identity disorder — to acknowledge that not everything which meaningfully exists has a metre attached to it. The mind belongs on a journey through scale even when it sits outside the ruler.
categories.ANCIENT_HISTORY.intro: Structures and artifacts whose engineering still invites careful explanation rather than easy dismissal. The Great Pyramid is the only stop here so far — but at 139 metres, with 2.3 million blocks aligned to the cardinal directions, it sits at exactly the right scale to bridge the human and the planetary.
categories.EARTH.description: Living things and landscapes on our own planet — from a half-millimetre water bear to the blue whale and the roof of the world.
categories.PHYSICS.description: Gravity, time, ripples in spacetime and quantum links — the rules that every object on the journey has to obey.
categories.EARTH.intro: The stretch of the scale you can actually touch. Life on Earth spans more than seven orders of magnitude — from a tardigrade you'd need a microscope to see, through a human being, to a blue whale longer than a basketball court — and the planet's own surface adds Mount Everest, almost nine kilometres of rock folded upward by colliding continents. These stops anchor the cosmic numbers to things you already have a feel for.
categories.PHYSICS.intro: Not objects but the rules behind them. Gravity, the weakest force, still decides the shape of everything from planets to galaxy clusters; time itself runs at different speeds depending on how fast you move and how deep you sit in a gravity well; spacetime can ripple, and on paper it can even fold into a wormhole. These stops have no size you could put on a ruler — what they have is reach: every other stop on the journey obeys them.

quark.name: Quark
quark.tagline: A fundamental building block of matter — with no measurable size at all.
quark.body: Quarks are point-like particles bound together by the strong force. They build up protons and neutrons — and through them, every atom in your body. Quarks have never been seen alone; they always travel in tight groups, held by gluons whose grip doesn't weaken as you pull them apart. Pull hard enough and the energy simply creates new quarks instead of freeing one.
quark.narrative: A quark is so small that even if a single atom were blown up to the size of Earth, a quark inside it would be at most the size of a grapefruit — and it may have no size at all.
quark.funFact: Quarks come in six flavours — up, down, charm, strange, top, bottom — and three colour charges that have nothing to do with light. Physicists named them with deliberate humour.

image.alt: A glowing quark suspended inside a gluon field.

facts.fact1: The heaviest, the top quark, weighs nearly as much as an entire gold atom.
facts.fact2: Carry a fractional electric charge — either ±1/3 or ±2/3.
facts.fact3: Always confined inside hadrons — never observed alone.
facts.fact4: Proposed independently by Gell-Mann and Zweig in 1964.
facts.fact5: Counterintuitive — climbing scale by powers of ten, you reach the edge of the observable universe in about 27 jumps from a human, but only 18 jumps down to a quark. We are closer in scale to a quark than to the cosmic horizon.

proton.name: Proton
proton.tagline: Three quarks bound into one of nature's most stable forms.
proton.body: A proton is a tiny ball of three quarks — two up and one down — held together by a roaring sea of gluons. Stack enough of them together with neutrons and electrons and you build every element from hydrogen to uranium. Protons appear so stable that we have never measured one decay.
proton.narrative: If a proton were the size of a basketball, the atom it lives inside would be wider than a small city.
proton.funFact: A free proton has never been observed to decay. The current lower limit on its lifetime is more than 10³⁴ years — about a trillion trillion times the age of the universe.

image.alt: A proton rendered as three glowing quarks bound by gluons.

facts.fact1: Made of two up quarks and one down quark.
facts.fact2: About 1,836 times the mass of an electron.
facts.fact3: Radius about 0.84 femtometres — less than a trillionth of a millimetre.
facts.fact4: Discovered by Ernest Rutherford in 1917.

atom.name: Atom
atom.tagline: The smallest piece of any chemical element.
atom.body: An atom is almost entirely empty space — a dense nucleus surrounded by a cloud of electrons that doesn't really orbit so much as exist as a probability. The character of every material around you, from oxygen to gold, comes from how many protons sit in that nucleus and how the electron cloud is shaped.
atom.narrative: If an atom were a marble in your palm, a single human hair beside it would be more than ten kilometres thick — as wide as a city.
atom.funFact: Strip away an atom's empty space and pack the nuclei together — and the entire human race would fit inside a sugar cube. The rest of you is mostly nothing.

image.alt: A hydrogen atom: a glowing nucleus inside a probabilistic electron cloud.

facts.fact1: More than 99.99% empty space.
facts.fact2: Number of protons defines the chemical element.
facts.fact3: Smallest unit that retains an element's chemical identity.
facts.fact4: Greek átomos — "uncuttable". Individual atoms were first seen in 1955, with a field-ion microscope.

dna.name: DNA
dna.tagline: The instruction book that builds you — and nearly every other living thing.
dna.body: DNA is the instruction book your body uses to build you. Nearly every cell carries the same complete copy — your eye colour, your height, the chance you'll inherit your father's allergies, all written into roughly two metres of DNA coiled inside that one cell. Reading those instructions is so reliable that a single hair, a stamp licked decades ago, or a cigarette butt left at a crime scene can identify exactly who it came from — which is why DNA has solved cases the police had given up on forty years earlier.
dna.narrative: If a single strand of DNA were as thick as a human hair, a flu virus alongside it would be about the size of a peppercorn.
dna.massNarrative: A single cell's DNA weighs about six trillionths of a gram, yet codes for an entire person. All the DNA across your roughly thirty trillion cells together weighs less than half a kilo.
dna.funFact: You and a chimpanzee share about 98.8% of your DNA — and around 60% of your genes even have a recognisable counterpart in a banana. Any two unrelated humans on the planet — strangers, neighbours, anyone — are 99.9% genetically identical. Everything you call 'different about people' is written in less than a tenth of one percent of your genome.

image.alt: A glowing double-helix DNA strand drifting through cellular space.

facts.fact1: Identical twins share virtually all their DNA — but not their fingerprints, which form by chance in the womb.
facts.fact2: Most Europeans and Asians carry roughly 1–2% Neanderthal DNA, inherited from interbreeding ~50,000 years ago.
facts.fact3: Each of your cells takes tens of thousands of hits to its DNA every day and repairs nearly all of them. Cancer typically starts when several uncorrected errors pile up in the same cell.
facts.fact4: Mitochondrial DNA passes only from mother to child — you can trace your direct maternal line back roughly 150,000 years to a single woman in Africa, nicknamed 'Mitochondrial Eve'.
facts.fact5: Roughly two metres of DNA is coiled into nearly every cell in your body, inside a nucleus a few thousandths of a millimetre across — like packing 20 km of fine thread into a tennis ball.
facts.fact6: The double helix was figured out in 1953. Rosalind Franklin's X-ray image (Photo 51) was central evidence — but she died before the 1962 Nobel Prize was awarded for the discovery.

mpd.name: Dissociative Identity Disorder
mpd.tagline: When the same brain hosts more than one self.
mpd.body: DID — once called Multiple Personality Disorder — is a documented psychological condition where distinct identities take turns in control of one body. The strangeness goes deeper than personality: clinicians have reported cases — mostly individual case studies — where one alter has measurable allergies, requires glasses, or shows different blood pressure, while another, in the same body, does not. The mind, somehow, may be voting on the body.
mpd.narrative: DID is a phenomenon of the mind, not a measurable object — its scale is psychological, not physical.
mpd.funFact: In the leading clinical model, DID emerges as the mind's protective response to severe childhood trauma. The 'alters' don't appear out of nowhere — they are parts of one self that learned, very early, that it was safer to compartmentalise than to be whole.

image.alt: A human silhouette splitting into multiple translucent overlapping personas.

facts.fact1: Recognised by the DSM since 1980.
facts.fact2: Often follows severe childhood trauma.
facts.fact3: Alters have been reported to show different allergies, eyesight, even handedness.
facts.fact4: Average time to a correct diagnosis: 5 to 12 years.

pyramid.name: The Great Pyramid
pyramid.tagline: 139 metres of limestone we still can't fully explain.
pyramid.body: The Great Pyramid of Giza is mainstream-dated to roughly 2560 BCE as a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu. The engineering — 2.3 million blocks, near-perfect cardinal alignment, a base level to within about two centimetres — keeps inviting alternative theories about its purpose. Most are speculative; the construction itself, though, is undeniably real.
pyramid.narrative: Roughly the height of a 45-storey building — the Great Pyramid stood as the tallest human structure for nearly four thousand years.
pyramid.funFact: The Great Pyramid is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing. Every other has fallen, burned, or been lost.

image.alt: The Great Pyramid of Giza at twilight, starlight aligning with its apex.

facts.fact1: Built around 2560 BCE — over 4,500 years old.
facts.fact2: 139 m tall today; originally 146.6 m before its casing eroded.
facts.fact3: Roughly 2.3 million stone blocks, 2.5 to 80 tonnes each.
facts.fact4: The tallest human-made structure for more than 3,800 years.

earth.name: Earth
earth.tagline: Our home planet — and this journey's reference grain of sand.
earth.body: If we shrink Earth down to a single 0.5 mm grain of sand, every other size in this journey changes by the same factor. At that scale the Sun is a billiard ball about six metres away, the Moon is a smaller speck just 1.5 cm from Earth, and the Milky Way spans about 40 million kilometres — a hundred real Earth–Moon distances. The trick is letting your sense of scale stretch.
earth.narrative: Quantumaire's anchor: if Earth were a single grain of sand, the Moon would be a smaller speck about 1.5 cm away, and the Sun would be a billiard ball roughly 6 metres off.
earth.massNarrative: Earth weighs about a 6 followed by 21 zeros — in tonnes. Compress that into a peanut and you'd have a black hole.
earth.funFact: Earth's day is slowly getting longer. When the first dinosaurs walked the planet, a day was less than 23 hours long; in a billion years it'll be over 25 hours.

image.alt: Earth seen from deep space, oceans and clouds glowing.

facts.fact1: Mean diameter: 12,742 km (12,756 km at the equator).
facts.fact2: Age: about 4.54 billion years.
facts.fact3: 70.8% of the surface is water.
facts.fact4: Magnetic field reverses, on average, every 200 to 300 thousand years.

neutron_star.name: Neutron Star
neutron_star.tagline: A city-sized star with the mass of a sun.
neutron_star.body: When a massive star collapses, its core can be crushed until protons and electrons merge into neutrons. The result is roughly 20 km across but weighs more than the Sun. A spinning, magnetised neutron star is called a pulsar — its lighthouse beams sweep past Earth with the regularity of an atomic clock.
neutron_star.narrative: A neutron star is roughly the diameter of a city — yet packs more mass than the entire Sun into that space.
neutron_star.massNarrative: A single sugar cube of neutron-star matter would outweigh every human on Earth combined.
neutron_star.funFact: A typical neutron star's surface sits at around 600,000 K (about 600,000 °C — at stellar temperatures the two scales are essentially the same), more than 100 times hotter than the surface of the Sun. Most of that heat radiates as X-rays our eyes can't see.

image.alt: A pulsar — a spinning neutron star with twin jets of radiation.

facts.fact1: Around 20 km across — yet heavier than the Sun.
facts.fact2: Surface gravity is roughly 10¹¹ × Earth's.
facts.fact3: The fastest known pulsar spins 716 times every second.
facts.fact4: Forms when a 10 to 25 solar-mass star collapses in a supernova.

sun.name: The Sun
sun.tagline: A self-sustaining fusion engine at the heart of our system.
sun.body: The Sun fuses 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second. The light reaching you right now took 8 minutes to cross the gap — but it took roughly 100,000 years to fight its way out from the Sun's dense core. Yet a cubic metre of that core releases only about 280 watts — less heat than the same volume of your own body. The Sun shines because it is enormous, not because its fusion is fierce.
sun.narrative: If the Sun were a basketball, Earth would be a peppercorn 26 metres away — and Pluto would be a dust mote a kilometre off.
sun.ifDistance: Light from the Sun reaches Earth in 8 minutes 20 seconds. At airline speeds, the journey would take 19 years. If you scale that 150-million-kilometre gap down to a single metre, Earth itself shrinks to less than a tenth of a millimetre — about the width of a human hair.
sun.massNarrative: The Sun holds 99.86% of all the mass in our Solar System. Every planet, moon, asteroid and comet combined is dust by comparison.
sun.funFact: Our Sun is often called an average star, yet it outshines roughly nine in ten stars in the Milky Way — most are dim red dwarfs. The largest red supergiants are around a thousand times wider, and the brightest blue stars pump out the light of millions of Suns.

image.alt: The Sun in ultraviolet — roiling plasma and arcing prominences.

facts.fact1: Fuses 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium each second.
facts.fact2: Sunlight takes 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth.
facts.fact3: Surface temperature 5,772 K (≈ 5,500 °C); core about 15.7 million K.
facts.fact4: Has been a main-sequence star for about 4.6 billion years.

uy_scuti.name: UY Scuti
uy_scuti.tagline: If it replaced the Sun, its surface would reach past Mars.
uy_scuti.body: UY Scuti is a red hypergiant so puffed up that its convection cells — single rising bubbles of hot gas on its surface — may be wider than Earth's entire orbit. Its outer layers are thinner than Earth's atmosphere; you could fly through them in a heat-proof ship and barely notice resistance. Stars this massive don't last long; UY Scuti will most likely end in a brilliant supernova.
uy_scuti.narrative: Hypergiants like UY Scuti live only a moment by cosmic standards — under ten million years from birth to supernova. Our Sun, ten times less massive, is already 4.6 billion years old and only about halfway done.
uy_scuti.ifDistance: The light we see from UY Scuti tonight left it about 5,900 years ago — when the first cities were only beginning to rise in Mesopotamia. Light leaving UY Scuti now won't reach Earth until generations of our descendants have come and gone.
uy_scuti.massNarrative: Despite being hundreds of times wider than the Sun, UY Scuti probably weighs only about seven to ten Suns. Most of its volume is near-vacuum — a giant balloon held up by pressure, not density.
uy_scuti.funFact: UY Scuti may already have exploded: its light takes about 5,900 years to reach us, so we simply wouldn't know yet. When it does go, it will briefly shine with the light of hundreds of millions of Suns.

image.alt: UY Scuti — a swollen red hypergiant, with the Sun shown for scale.

facts.fact1: Radius about 909 × the Sun's (2023 estimate) — older figures of ~1,700 were revised down with Gaia distances.
facts.fact2: Light takes about 70 minutes to cross UY Scuti from one side to the other — longer than sunlight takes to reach Jupiter.
facts.fact3: Brightness varies by more than 2 magnitudes over a cycle of roughly 740 days.
facts.fact4: Lies about 5,900 light-years away in the constellation Scutum.

milky_way.name: Milky Way
milky_way.tagline: A barred spiral of hundreds of billions of stars — including ours.
milky_way.body: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy about 100,000 light-years across. Our Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in it, riding a quiet arm called Orion. At the very centre is Sagittarius A* — a supermassive black hole four million times the mass of the Sun.
milky_way.narrative: If the Milky Way were shrunk to the size of France, the entire Solar System would fit inside a coin.
milky_way.massNarrative: The visible stars are just a few percent of the Milky Way's total mass. The rest — around 90% — is invisible dark matter.
milky_way.funFact: We cannot see the Milky Way's centre with visible light — interstellar dust blocks the view. Infrared and radio telescopes are what proved Sagittarius A* is there.

image.alt: The Milky Way galaxy seen face-on, spiral arms glowing.

facts.fact1: More than 100,000 light-years across.
facts.fact2: Contains an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars.
facts.fact3: Sagittarius A* at the centre is a 4-million-solar-mass black hole.
facts.fact4: Our Sun orbits the galactic centre roughly every 230 million years.

milky_way.insideNote: We're inside it — about 26,000 light-years from its centre

dark_matter.name: Dark Matter
dark_matter.tagline: Invisible mass that holds galaxies together — and we don't know what it is.
dark_matter.body: Galaxies spin too fast for the matter we can see to hold them together — they should be flying apart. Something invisible is providing the extra gravity. We can map it through gravitational lensing, and it appears to outweigh ordinary matter five to one. We just don't know what it is.
dark_matter.narrative: Dark matter has no shape and no edges that we can see — only its gravity is visible, shaping the rotation of nearly every galaxy ever measured.
dark_matter.funFact: If dark matter is made of particles, as most physicists suspect, billions of them may be streaming through your body every second. They barely interact with the atoms in you, if at all — so you never notice.

image.alt: Dark matter visualised as a violet cosmic web bending light around galaxies.

facts.fact1: About 27% of the universe's total mass-energy.
facts.fact2: Roughly five times the mass of all ordinary matter combined.
facts.fact3: Detected indirectly via galaxy rotation curves and lensing.
facts.fact4: No particle of dark matter has ever been directly detected.

dark_energy.name: Dark Energy
dark_energy.tagline: Whatever is pulling the universe apart, faster and faster.
dark_energy.body: The expansion of the universe isn't just continuing — it's accelerating. A mysterious form of energy, present in every cubic metre of empty space, seems to be pushing it outward. It accounts for roughly 68% of everything there is, and we have almost no idea what it is made of.
dark_energy.narrative: Dark energy fills every cubic metre of empty space — including the metres around you right now. It has no size of its own, only a direction: outward.
dark_energy.funFact: The term 'dark energy' was coined in 1998 by cosmologist Michael Turner — chosen specifically because nobody knew what it was. Almost 30 years later, the placeholder name has held up because we still don't.

image.alt: Galaxies stretching apart, pulled by an invisible accelerating force.

facts.fact1: About 68% of the universe's total mass-energy.
facts.fact2: Discovered in 1998 via supernova measurements of cosmic expansion.
facts.fact3: Simplest description is Einstein's cosmological constant Λ — though DESI survey data (2024–25) hint it may be weakening over time.
facts.fact4: Drives the universe's accelerating expansion.

observable_universe.name: Observable Universe
observable_universe.tagline: The 93-billion-light-year sphere we can, in principle, see.
observable_universe.body: The observable universe is everything close enough that light has had time to reach us since the Big Bang. It is a sphere about 93 billion light-years across — and almost certainly a tiny slice of something larger. Past its edge, the rest is forever beyond our horizon.
observable_universe.narrative: Light from the edge of the observable universe has been travelling for the entire 13.8 billion years of cosmic history to reach us — and at the same time, more space keeps appearing in between.
observable_universe.massNarrative: Most of the universe's mass-energy isn't ordinary matter at all — roughly 68% is dark energy, 27% is dark matter, and only 5% is everything you can see.
observable_universe.funFact: By most measures, the Milky Way is a fairly large galaxy. Most of the galaxies in the observable universe — hundreds of billions, perhaps as many as 2 trillion — are smaller than ours.

image.alt: The observable universe as a luminous sphere of galaxies and cosmic web.

facts.fact1: Roughly 93 billion light-years in diameter.
facts.fact2: Contains hundreds of billions of galaxies — estimates run as high as 2 trillion.
facts.fact3: Light from its edge has travelled for about 13.8 billion years.
facts.fact4: Space itself can — and does — expand faster than light.
facts.fact5: Take the smallest meaningful length in physics — the Planck length, around 10⁻³⁵ m — and the diameter of the observable universe. A human sits roughly in the middle of that scale, slightly closer to the cosmic side. We are not big or small. We are scaled to notice both.

virus.name: Virus
virus.tagline: Strands of code wrapped in protein.
virus.body: A virus is not strictly alive. It has no metabolism, can't reproduce on its own, and shows no behaviour outside a host. What it carries is a packet of genetic instructions — DNA or RNA — inside a protein shell. Once inside a cell, those instructions hijack the host's machinery and turn it into a copy factory.
virus.narrative: Magnify a virus to the size of a marble in your palm — at that scale, a typical human cell would stand about as tall as you.
virus.funFact: There are an estimated 10³¹ virus particles on Earth — about ten million times more than there are stars in the entire observable universe.

image.alt: An icosahedral virus capsid glowing in cyan and violet, RNA visible inside.

facts.fact1: Most are smaller than a wavelength of visible light.
facts.fact2: Cannot reproduce outside a host cell.
facts.fact3: Genetic material can be DNA or RNA, single- or double-stranded.
facts.fact4: First identified as a "filterable agent" by Ivanovsky in 1892.

supermassive_black_hole.name: Sagittarius A*
supermassive_black_hole.tagline: The supermassive black hole at the heart of our galaxy — and its more extreme cousins.
supermassive_black_hole.body: Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*) is the supermassive black hole at the centre of the Milky Way, about 4.15 million solar masses packed into a region 24 million km across — comfortably inside Mercury's orbit. It's modest by black-hole standards: TON 618 and Phoenix-A weigh tens of billions of solar masses each. Our nearest known black hole of any kind, Gaia BH1, is a much smaller stellar-mass one only 1,560 light-years away. The first direct images of supermassive black holes came in 2019 (M87*) and 2022 (Sgr A* itself).
supermassive_black_hole.narrative: Sagittarius A*'s event horizon is wide enough to swallow 17 Suns lined up edge to edge — yet it would still fit comfortably inside Mercury's orbit around our own Sun.
supermassive_black_hole.massNarrative: Sagittarius A* packs the mass of 4.15 million Suns into that region — and it's a modest example; the largest known supermassive black holes weigh tens of billions of Suns.
supermassive_black_hole.funFact: We weighed Sagittarius A* by watching stars orbit it. One, S2, completes a lap every 16 years and whips past the black hole at about 2.5% of the speed of light — work that earned Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez a share of the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics.

image.alt: A supermassive black hole — a black sphere ringed by a glowing accretion disk.

facts.fact1: Sagittarius A* — about 4.15 million solar masses.
facts.fact2: Event horizon roughly 24 million km across.
facts.fact3: First direct image: M87* in 2019; Sagittarius A* in 2022.
facts.fact4: Nothing — not even light — can escape from inside the event horizon.

bacterium.name: Bacterium
bacterium.body: Bacteria are the workhorse cells of the planet. They have no nucleus — their DNA floats free in the cytoplasm — and they replicate by splitting in half, sometimes every twenty minutes. The human body holds roughly as many bacterial cells as human ones, and they outnumber every kind of multicellular life put together.
bacterium.narrative: Magnify a bacterium until it sits in your palm like a marble — and a single grain of sand at that same scale would be a boulder nearly four metres high.
bacterium.funFact: By count, roughly half of all the cells in your body are bacteria. By mass, they only add up to a couple of hundred grams — but without them you couldn't digest a meal.

image.alt: A single rod-shaped bacterium with flagella trailing through aqueous medium.

facts.fact1: Most are about 0.5–5 micrometres long, depending on the species.
facts.fact2: No nucleus — they are prokaryotes.
facts.fact3: Reproduce by binary fission, sometimes every 20 minutes.
facts.fact4: Your gut holds roughly 38 trillion bacterial cells.

galaxy_cluster.name: Virgo Cluster
galaxy_cluster.tagline: The nearest large galaxy cluster — over a thousand galaxies bound by gravity.
galaxy_cluster.body: The Virgo Cluster is the dense centre of our local galactic neighbourhood — around 1,500 galaxies bound together by gravity, spread across a region about 15 million light-years wide and about 54 million light-years from us. The Milky Way and Andromeda sit on the outskirts of the wider supercluster it anchors. Larger clusters exist: the Coma Cluster holds over 1,000 galaxies in a denser concentration, and the Phoenix Cluster is one of the most massive ever measured. Past the cluster scale, structures stop being gravitationally bound and stretch into superclusters.
galaxy_cluster.narrative: A galaxy cluster is so wide that light needs around fifteen million years just to cross it — longer than the entire time the human genus has existed on Earth.
galaxy_cluster.massNarrative: A big cluster like Virgo weighs about a thousand trillion Suns — and most of that mass, again, is dark matter rather than stars.
galaxy_cluster.funFact: Galaxy clusters in our neighbourhood are all being pulled toward an unseen mass concentration — the so-called Great Attractor — sitting at the heart of the Laniakea Supercluster.

image.alt: A galaxy cluster — dozens of galaxies around a bright central giant elliptical.

facts.fact1: Hundreds to thousands of galaxies bound by gravity.
facts.fact2: Typically a few million to tens of millions of light-years across.
facts.fact3: Holds far more mass in hot gas than in stars — and even more in dark matter.
facts.fact4: Virgo, our nearest cluster, lies about 54 million light-years away.

andromeda.name: Andromeda
andromeda.tagline: Our nearest large galactic neighbour — and a possible future collision partner.
andromeda.body: Andromeda is a spiral galaxy about 2.5 million light-years away — close enough to see with the naked eye on a dark night, as a faint smudge in the constellation of the same name. It holds something like a trillion stars, more than the Milky Way. The two galaxies are closing in at about 110 km/s and may one day merge into a single elliptical galaxy nicknamed Milkomeda — though a 2025 study puts the odds of that happening within 10 billion years at only about 50:50.
andromeda.narrative: Andromeda already covers about six full moons in our night sky — yet its light has travelled 2.5 million years to reach us. You're seeing it as it was before the first members of our genus, Homo, appeared.
andromeda.ifDistance: If you could fly to Andromeda at the speed of light, the trip out and back would take five million years — longer than the entire age of the human genus on Earth. Slow it down to Voyager 1's 17 km/s — the fastest anything we've built is leaving the Solar System — and the one-way trip alone takes about 44 billion years, three times the current age of the universe.
andromeda.massNarrative: Andromeda and the Milky Way are roughly matched in mass — each about a trillion Suns, most of it in an unseen dark-matter halo.
andromeda.funFact: Andromeda is one of the few galaxies actually moving toward us. Cosmic expansion is normally winning, but our gravitational bond with Andromeda is winning here.

image.alt: The Andromeda galaxy seen at an angle, full spiral arms and bright core visible.

facts.fact1: About 2.5 million light-years away — naked-eye visible.
facts.fact2: Contains roughly 1 trillion stars (more than the Milky Way).
facts.fact3: Approaching us at about 110 km/s.
facts.fact4: Chance of merging with the Milky Way within 10 billion years: about 50% (2025 Hubble + Gaia study).

cell.name: Cell
cell.body: A cell is where chemistry becomes biology — a membrane-bound bag of molecules that can copy itself. Your body holds about 30 trillion of them. Many bacteria are just 1–2 µm long; a human red blood cell is about 8 µm across; some single cells, like an ostrich egg yolk, are large enough to hold in your hand.
cell.narrative: Scale a cell up to the size of a basketball — at that same scale, a single human hair would be a pillar nearly two metres thick.
cell.funFact: Your body replaces about 330 billion cells every day — nearly four million every second, most of them blood cells.

image.alt: A cross-section of a eukaryotic cell — membrane, nucleus, and organelles glowing.

facts.fact1: The human body contains about 30 trillion cells.
facts.fact2: Smallest bacterium is about 200 nanometres across.
facts.fact3: Often cited as the largest single cell: an ostrich egg yolk, around 75 mm.
facts.fact4: First described by Robert Hooke in 1665, observing thin slices of cork.

human.name: Human
human.tagline: Halfway between the smallest and the largest — on a logarithmic scale.
human.body: A 1.7-metre human sits surprisingly close to the middle of everything. Count the powers of ten from the Planck length — the smallest length physics can meaningfully talk about — to the edge of the observable universe: there are about 62, and you sit roughly 35 up. By mass the coincidence is even neater. The middle turns out to be a remarkably comfortable place to think from.
human.narrative: By mass, you sit almost exactly midway between a proton and a star: the Sun outweighs you by about as many powers of ten as you outweigh a proton.
human.funFact: Almost every hydrogen nucleus in your body formed within the first second after the Big Bang. Everything heavier than helium was forged inside stars that lived and died before our Sun was born.

image.alt: A human silhouette against a vertical cosmic gradient suggesting scale.

facts.fact1: Average adult height is about 1.7 metres.
facts.fact2: Your mass sits near the geometric mean of a proton (10⁻²⁷ kg) and the Sun (10³⁰ kg).
facts.fact3: Your body holds roughly 7 × 10²⁷ atoms — more than the number of stars in the universe.
facts.fact4: Human bone is, by weight, about four times stronger than concrete.

light_year.name: Light-Year
light_year.tagline: The distance a single beam of light covers in one year.
light_year.body: A light-year is a unit of distance, not time. At roughly 300,000 km per second, light covers about 9.46 trillion kilometres in a year — about 63,241 astronomical units. Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun, lies 4.24 light-years away. Even at the Voyager probes' speed, reaching it would take more than 70,000 years.
light_year.narrative: The distance light travels in a year. Even Voyager — the farthest space probe humans have ever flown — would need over 17,000 years to cover it.
light_year.funFact: Galaxies hold hundreds of billions of stars, yet typical pairs of stars are several light-years apart. By volume, a galaxy is almost entirely empty space.

image.alt: A beam of light stretching toward a distant binary star system.

facts.fact1: Equal to about 9.46 trillion kilometres.
facts.fact2: About 63,241 astronomical units.
facts.fact3: Proxima Centauri — the nearest star — is 4.24 light-years away.
facts.fact4: Professional astronomy more often uses parsecs (1 pc ≈ 3.26 ly).

ton_618.name: TON 618
ton_618.tagline: An ultramassive quasar — one of the largest black holes ever measured.
ton_618.body: TON 618 is a quasar — an actively feeding supermassive black hole — at the heart of a distant galaxy whose light has travelled about 10.8 billion years to reach Earth. Its mass is estimated at around 40 billion solar masses, with an event horizon roughly 1,600 astronomical units across. The light we see from it left when our Sun did not yet exist; what TON 618 looks like now, no one will ever know.
ton_618.narrative: If our Sun were a marble, TON 618's event horizon at the same scale would be about 2.5 kilometres across — a marble beside a small town.
ton_618.massNarrative: TON 618 weighs around 40 billion Suns — ten thousand times the mass of Sagittarius A* at the centre of our galaxy. How black holes this large grew so early in cosmic history is one of the open puzzles of cosmology.

image.alt: TON 618 — a colossal black hole ringed by a vast accretion disk, polar jets shooting out into space.

facts.fact1: Estimated mass: ~40 billion solar masses.
facts.fact2: Event horizon roughly 1,600 AU across — about 20 times the width of Pluto's orbit.
facts.fact3: Light-travel distance: about 10.8 billion light-years.
facts.fact4: Catalogued in 1957 as a faint blue 'star'; revealed as a distant quasar in the 1970s.

ton_618.funFact: TON 618 is a hyperluminous quasar — its accretion disk shines with the brightness of 140 trillion Suns, which is how we can see it across most of the visible universe.

phoenix_a.name: Phoenix-A
phoenix_a.tagline: At the heart of the Phoenix Cluster — among the most massive known black holes.
phoenix_a.body: Phoenix-A is the supermassive black hole at the centre of the Phoenix Cluster, whose light has travelled about 5.8 billion years to reach us. Its mass is among the largest ever estimated, but the estimates disagree wildly — from a few billion to about 100 billion solar masses. Here we use a mid-range figure of about 25 billion. The host cluster is famous for its extraordinarily luminous central galaxy and one of the highest star-formation rates ever observed in a brightest-cluster galaxy.
phoenix_a.narrative: If our Sun were a marble, Phoenix-A's event horizon at the same scale would be about 1.6 kilometres across — wide enough to line up more than 100,000 Suns edge to edge.
phoenix_a.massNarrative: Around 25 billion solar masses on our working estimate — roughly 6,000 times the mass of Sagittarius A* at the centre of our galaxy. Mass estimates for objects this distant carry wide error bars; published values run from a few billion to about 100 billion solar masses.

image.alt: Phoenix-A — an enormous black hole inside a luminous galaxy cluster, intracluster gas glowing around it.

facts.fact1: Mass: published estimates range from a few billion to ~100 billion solar masses; we use ~25 billion.
facts.fact2: Host: the Phoenix Cluster, whose light has travelled ~5.8 billion years to reach us.
facts.fact3: Surrounded by one of the hottest, brightest intracluster gas concentrations ever measured.
facts.fact4: The Phoenix Cluster's central galaxy forms roughly 500–800 Suns' worth of new stars every year — hundreds of times the Milky Way's rate.

phoenix_a.funFact: In most giant clusters, the central black hole's outbursts act like a thermostat, keeping the hot gas from cooling into stars. In Phoenix that thermostat seems to be failing — gas is cooling fast and the central galaxy is forming stars at a ferocious rate, a puzzle astronomers are still working out.

voyager1.name: Voyager 1
voyager1.tagline: The farthest human-made object — and still calling home.
voyager1.body: Voyager 1 launched from Cape Canaveral in September 1977 on a mission to fly past Jupiter and Saturn. Forty-nine years later it's still operating — now in interstellar space, more than 173 astronomical units from Earth, sending back a faint trickle of data on the particles and magnetic fields around it. In November 2026 it became the first human-made object one light-day from Earth: every signal now takes a full day to arrive.
voyager1.narrative: Voyager 1 is so far away that a radio command from Earth takes a full day to reach it. Yet on the scale of the stars it has barely left home: even at 61,000 km/h it needs about 17,600 years to cover a single light-year — and the nearest star is more than four light-years away.
voyager1.ifDistance: A radio signal from Earth now takes a full day to reach Voyager 1. If you shrank that gap to the length of a football pitch (105 m), the Earth–Sun distance would be about 60 centimetres — and the nearest star would still be more than 160 kilometres away.

image.alt: Voyager 1 spacecraft against the cosmic void, dish antenna pointing back toward a distant Earth.

facts.fact1: Launched 5 September 1977 — over 49 years ago.
facts.fact2: About 26 billion km from Earth — more than 173 astronomical units.
facts.fact3: Radio signals take about 24 hours each way — it passed one light-day from Earth on 18 November 2026.
facts.fact4: Carries the Golden Record — sounds and images of Earth, for any future finder.
facts.fact5: Speed: about 17 km/s — roughly 61,000 km/h relative to the Sun.
facts.fact6: At that speed, crossing a single light-year would take about 17,600 years.

voyager1.massNarrative: Voyager 1 weighs about 720 kg — roughly as much as a dairy cow. It and its twin, Voyager 2, are the only human-made objects known to have crossed into interstellar space.
voyager1.funFact: Voyager 1 isn't aimed at any particular star. In about 40,000 years it will pass within 1.6 light-years of Gliese 445 — but by then the constellations we know will have rearranged themselves.

laniakea_supercluster.name: Laniakea Supercluster
laniakea_supercluster.tagline: The supercluster of galaxy clusters our Milky Way lives inside.
laniakea_supercluster.body: Laniakea is the vast supercluster of which our Milky Way is a tiny outer participant. It spans roughly 500 million light-years and contains about 100,000 galaxies organised along filaments that all stream toward a common gravitational basin — the Great Attractor. Astronomers only formally identified Laniakea in 2014. Even larger structures exist out there, such as the contentious Hercules-Corona Borealis Great Wall, but no supercluster is truly bound by gravity — cosmic expansion is gradually pulling them apart.
laniakea_supercluster.narrative: If the Milky Way were a grain of rice, Laniakea would be about the size of a concert hall — a hall scattered with a hundred thousand grains, each one a galaxy, all drifting toward the same hidden pull.

image.alt: Laniakea Supercluster — a sprawling web of galaxies flowing toward a central gravitational basin.

facts.fact1: Around 500 million light-years across.
facts.fact2: Contains roughly 100,000 galaxies.
facts.fact3: All flow toward the Great Attractor at its centre.
facts.fact4: Formally defined only in 2014.

laniakea_supercluster.massNarrative: It would take about 30 billion trillion Earths to match Laniakea's mass — and yet it isn't truly bound together: cosmic expansion is slowly pulling it apart.
laniakea_supercluster.funFact: The name "Laniakea" was chosen in honour of the Polynesian navigators who crossed the Pacific by reading the stars; in Hawaiian it means "immeasurable heaven."

solar_system.name: The Solar System
solar_system.tagline: One star and everything held in its gravity.
solar_system.body: Eight planets, five dwarf planets, more than 400 moons, and millions of asteroids and comets — all bound to one yellow star. The planetary part is roughly 12 billion km wide. The Sun's gravity, though, reaches out thousands of times further, into a faint shell of icy bodies called the Oort cloud. Voyager 1, our farthest probe, has been travelling for 49 years and hasn't even reached it yet.
solar_system.narrative: Shrink the Solar System out to Neptune's orbit to fit on a basketball court, and Earth would be smaller than a grain of sand near the centre — completely invisible to the naked eye.
solar_system.massNarrative: The Sun holds 99.86% of the Solar System's entire mass. Pile every planet, moon, asteroid, and comet together and you get just 0.14% — and most of that is Jupiter.
solar_system.funFact: Pluto isn't the last word: beyond the Kuiper Belt sits the Oort Cloud, a roughly spherical shell of icy bodies that may extend halfway to the nearest star. Voyager 1, our farthest probe, won't reach its inner edge for another 300 years and won't clear its outer edge for tens of thousands more.

image.alt: Top-down view of the Solar System — Sun centred, planets along orbital ellipses.

facts.fact1: Pluto orbits about 5.9 billion km from the Sun.
facts.fact2: 8 planets, 5 dwarf planets, more than 400 known moons.
facts.fact3: Voyager 1 has been travelling for 49 years and is about 26 billion km out.
facts.fact4: The Oort cloud may extend up to 100,000 AU from the Sun.
facts.fact5: Even at Jupiter's closest approach (opposition), it is still more than four times farther from us than the Sun is.

moon.name: The Moon
moon.tagline: Earth's only natural satellite — and the only other world humans have walked on.
moon.body: The Moon is the fifth-largest moon in the Solar System and the only place beyond Earth that humans have walked on. It is tidally locked, which is why the same side always faces us; the far side was first photographed by a Soviet probe in 1959. Its surface is a fossil record of the violent early Solar System — every crater is a story that Earth itself has long since erased through weather and tectonics.
moon.narrative: The Moon is drifting away from Earth at about 3.8 cm a year — roughly the rate your fingernails grow. Hundreds of millions of years ago, total solar eclipses lasted much longer; in roughly 600 million years, they'll stop happening at all.
moon.ifDistance: If you could drive a car non-stop at 100 km/h, reaching the Moon would take about 160 days. Walking at average human pace, you'd arrive in roughly nine years. The Apollo astronauts made the trip in three days each way, and Apollo 13's distance record stood for 56 years — until Artemis II's crew swung around the Moon in April 2026, 406,771 km from Earth.
moon.massNarrative: The Moon weighs about 1/81 of Earth — roughly a tennis ball next to a house cat. Among the planets' moons, it's the largest relative to its host.
moon.funFact: The Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the Moon. Laser pulses fired from observatories on Earth still bounce off them today, letting us measure the Earth–Moon distance to within millimetres.

image.alt: The Moon as a full disc, cratered surface lit by direct sunlight.

facts.fact1: Diameter about 3,475 km — roughly a quarter of Earth's.
facts.fact2: Average distance from Earth: 384,400 km.
facts.fact3: Tidally locked — the same hemisphere always faces Earth.
facts.fact4: Twelve humans have walked on its surface, all between 1969 and 1972.

jupiter.name: Jupiter
jupiter.tagline: The Solar System's largest planet — heavier than all the others combined.
jupiter.body: Jupiter is a gas giant more massive than all the other planets combined. Its atmosphere is a turbulent ocean of hydrogen and helium, marked by storm belts and the Great Red Spot — an anticyclone large enough to swallow Earth and still have room left over. It also has more than 100 known moons; four of them, the Galilean satellites, were the first objects ever shown to orbit something other than Earth.
jupiter.narrative: Jupiter is so massive that it doesn't orbit the Sun directly — the two share a common centre of mass, called the barycentre, that sits just outside the Sun's surface. It's the only planet in our system where this is true.
jupiter.ifDistance: Jupiter orbits about 5.2 times farther from the Sun than Earth does. Put the Sun — a golf ball at this scale — under one hoop of a basketball court, and Earth would circle 5 metres away while Jupiter sat near the far end, 26 metres out.
jupiter.massNarrative: Jupiter contains 2.5 times more mass than every other planet in the Solar System combined. The wobble it induces in the Sun is the strongest single planetary signal in our system — and is one of the standard ways astronomers find Jupiter-sized planets around other stars.
jupiter.funFact: If Jupiter had grown about 80 times more massive, hydrogen fusion would have ignited in its core and it would have become a small star. We would live in a binary system instead of a planetary one.

image.alt: Jupiter with banded cloud belts and the Great Red Spot, four Galilean moons visible beside it.

facts.fact1: Diameter about 139,820 km — roughly 11 times Earth's.
facts.fact2: Average distance from the Sun: 778 million km (about 5.2 AU).
facts.fact3: A day on Jupiter is under 10 hours — the fastest spin of any planet.
facts.fact4: More than 100 known moons (101 as of March 2026), including the four large Galilean satellites.

proxima_centauri.name: Proxima Centauri
proxima_centauri.tagline: The closest known star to the Sun — and still impossibly far.
proxima_centauri.body: Proxima Centauri is a small, dim red dwarf about 4.24 light-years from Earth. It is the nearest known star to the Sun, part of the triple Alpha Centauri system. At least two planets are confirmed to orbit it, one — Proxima b — sitting in the habitable zone where liquid water could exist on its surface. The catch is that red dwarfs are violently active; Proxima regularly fires off flares that could strip away an Earth-like atmosphere.
proxima_centauri.narrative: Even at the speed of light it takes 4.24 years to get to Proxima Centauri. The fastest human spacecraft ever launched (Parker Solar Probe) would take more than 6,000 years to make the trip.
proxima_centauri.ifDistance: Driving non-stop at highway speeds (100 km/h), the trip to Proxima Centauri would take roughly 45 million years — sixteen times longer than the human genus has existed. Light makes the journey in 4.24 years, but the fastest probe humans have ever built would still need more than six thousand.
proxima_centauri.massNarrative: Proxima Centauri weighs only about an eighth of the Sun. Red dwarfs that small fuse hydrogen so slowly that, in theory, Proxima will still be shining four trillion years from now — long after every Sun-like star has burned out.
proxima_centauri.funFact: Despite being our nearest stellar neighbour, Proxima is too dim to see with the naked eye. You need a telescope — even though, in cosmic terms, it's basically next door.

image.alt: Proxima Centauri — a small red dwarf star with the silhouette of Proxima b crossing its disc.

facts.fact1: About 4.24 light-years away — roughly 40 trillion km.
facts.fact2: Diameter about 214,000 km — about 15% of the Sun's.
facts.fact3: A red dwarf, with a surface temperature of around 3,000 K (≈ 2,700 °C).
facts.fact4: Has at least two known planets, including Proxima b in the habitable zone.

mars.name: Mars
mars.tagline: Earth's red neighbour — and our best shot at a second home.
mars.body: Mars is a cold, dusty world about half Earth's diameter, wrapped in an atmosphere so thin it's barely there. But the geology underneath is shockingly familiar: dry riverbeds, frozen polar caps, volcanoes bigger than any on Earth, and a canyon — Valles Marineris — so long it would stretch from New York to Los Angeles. We have rovers driving across it right now, and people planning to follow.
mars.narrative: Stand on Mars on a clear day and the sky is butterscotch-pink, the sunset is blue, and the sun looks two-thirds its usual size. Earth, when you spot it, is a bright blue star.
mars.ifDistance: When Mars is at its closest to Earth — once every two years or so — it's still about 140 times farther away than the Moon. A radio signal takes 3 minutes one-way at closest approach, and 22 minutes when Mars is on the far side of the Sun. Rovers have to think for themselves whenever they can't wait that long.
mars.funFact: Olympus Mons, the largest known volcano in the Solar System, is about 22 km tall — two and a half times the height of Mount Everest above sea level. Mars's weaker gravity and lack of plate tectonics let single volcanoes grow that big.

image.alt: Mars seen as a full disc from orbit — rust-coloured surface with a bright polar ice cap.

facts.fact1: Diameter 6,779 km — about half Earth's.
facts.fact2: Average distance from Earth ~225 million km — closest pass ~54 million km.
facts.fact3: Average surface temperature 210 K (≈ -63 °C); ranges from 130 K at the poles to 308 K at the equator at noon.
facts.fact4: Atmosphere is 95% CO₂ but less than 1% of Earth's air pressure.
facts.fact5: Hosts Olympus Mons (22 km tall) and Valles Marineris (4,000 km long) — both record-holders in the Solar System.

pluto.name: Pluto
pluto.tagline: A dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt — and far more alive than anyone expected.
pluto.body: Pluto is smaller than our Moon, orbits the Sun once every 248 years, and was demoted from planet to dwarf planet in 2006 — because we kept finding objects out there just like it. Then in 2015, NASA's New Horizons spacecraft flew past and showed us a world with nitrogen-ice plains, water-ice mountains, and a heart-shaped region called Tombaugh Regio that nobody had expected to see on something so far from the Sun.
pluto.narrative: Pluto's heart-shaped plain is geologically active — its surface is renewing itself even today, billions of kilometres from any warmth a star can provide. Whatever heats it, it isn't sunlight.
pluto.ifDistance: Sunlight takes 5.5 hours to reach Pluto. Stand on its surface at noon and the Sun looks like a particularly bright star — bright enough to read by, but small enough to cover with the head of a pin held at arm's length.
pluto.funFact: Pluto and its largest moon, Charon, are tidally locked to each other — they always show each other the same face. From Pluto, Charon never moves in the sky. It's a slow waltz partner that simply hangs there.

image.alt: Pluto in true colour — pale ice plains, the heart-shaped Tombaugh Regio, and reddish tholin terrain.

facts.fact1: Diameter 2,377 km — smaller than Earth's Moon.
facts.fact2: Average distance from Earth ~5.9 billion km; one Pluto year = 248 Earth years.
facts.fact3: Surface temperature around 44 K (≈ -229 °C) — cold enough to freeze nitrogen.
facts.fact4: Demoted from planet to dwarf planet in 2006 once similar-sized neighbours were found.
facts.fact5: Surface is geologically young — flowing nitrogen ice resurfaces it even now.

halley.name: Halley's Comet
halley.tagline: An icy visitor that returns every human lifetime.
halley.body: Halley's Comet is a peanut-shaped chunk of ice and dust about 15 km long, on a 76-year orbit that swings it from beyond Neptune to inside Venus's orbit. When it nears the Sun, the ice boils off and it grows two tails — one of dust, one of ionised gas — that stretch tens of millions of kilometres across the sky. Edmond Halley was the first to realise that comets seen in 1531, 1607, and 1682 were the same object returning. He predicted its 1758 comeback. He didn't live to see it, but it came.
halley.narrative: Most people see Halley's Comet at most twice in their lives. It last visited in 1986. Its next pass is due in 2061. The same chunk of ice has probably been doing this since before the pyramids.
halley.funFact: In 1986 ESA's Giotto flew within 600 km of Halley's nucleus. Dust impacts sent it wobbling and wrecked its camera — but not before it had captured the first close-up portrait of a comet's nucleus.

image.alt: Halley's Comet nucleus close-up — dark peanut-shaped body with bright jets of gas erupting toward the Sun.

facts.fact1: Nucleus is roughly 15 × 8 km — irregular, peanut-shaped.
facts.fact2: Orbital period: about 76 years. Last seen 1986; next expected ~2061.
facts.fact3: Surface is darker than coal — one of the darkest objects in the Solar System.
facts.fact4: Loses about a metre of surface ice each pass; will eventually fizzle out.
facts.fact5: First certain record: Chinese astronomers in 240 BCE. Every return since has been logged — 30 in all.

mercury.name: Mercury
mercury.tagline: The innermost planet — a cratered world of impossible extremes.
mercury.body: Mercury is the smallest planet in the Solar System and the closest to the Sun. Its surface looks remarkably like our Moon's: heavily cratered, airless, and grey. But the days swing between extremes a moon never sees — over 400 °C in direct sunlight, then dropping below -170 °C on the night side, because there's no atmosphere to hold the heat. And one Mercury day, sunrise to sunrise, lasts 176 Earth days — two of its 88-day years.
mercury.narrative: Stand on Mercury at noon and the Sun looks up to three times wider than from Earth, baking the rocks to over 400 °C. Wait for nightfall — 88 Earth days later — and the same ground sinks below -170 °C: a swing of nearly 600 degrees.
mercury.ifDistance: Sunlight takes only about 3 minutes to reach Mercury. From Earth, even at closest approach, Mercury is 77 million km away — a radio signal still takes more than four minutes to get there.
mercury.funFact: Despite being closest to the Sun, Mercury isn't the hottest planet — Venus is, because of its runaway greenhouse atmosphere. Mercury's polar craters even hold water ice, kept frozen in permanent shadow.

image.alt: Mercury as a full disc — heavily cratered grey surface, similar to Earth's Moon.

facts.fact1: Diameter 4,879 km — smaller than Jupiter's moon Ganymede.
facts.fact2: Year is 88 Earth days; solar day is 176 Earth days.
facts.fact3: Surface temperature swings from -173 °C at night to 427 °C in direct sunlight.
facts.fact4: Has no atmosphere to speak of and only the thinnest exosphere.
facts.fact5: Polar craters hold confirmed deposits of water ice in permanent shadow.

venus.name: Venus
venus.tagline: Earth's twin in size — and its opposite in everything else.
venus.body: Venus is almost exactly Earth's diameter, and the second planet from the Sun. From a distance the planet looks placid — wrapped in featureless cream-coloured clouds. But the atmosphere below is the most hostile in the Solar System: 96% carbon dioxide, sulphuric-acid clouds, a surface pressure 92 times Earth's, and a runaway greenhouse effect that keeps the rocks at 465 °C — hot enough to melt lead. No spacecraft has lasted more than two hours on its surface.
venus.narrative: Look for Venus tonight — the brightest point of light in the sky after the Moon. Then remember that under those innocent-looking clouds, the air would crush you, cook you, and dissolve what was left in acid, all at once.
venus.ifDistance: At closest approach Venus comes within 38 million km of Earth — closer than any other planet. Two-way radio signals take just over four minutes when the timing is right. Yet no human has ever even attempted to fly there.
venus.funFact: Venus rotates backwards relative to almost every other planet, and so slowly that one rotation (243 Earth days) takes longer than its year (225 Earth days). The Sun there rises in the west and sets in the east — with about 117 Earth days from one sunrise to the next.

image.alt: Venus as a full disc — pale cream-and-tan cloud bands wrapping the planet.

facts.fact1: Diameter 12,104 km — about 95% of Earth's.
facts.fact2: Surface temperature ~465 °C — the hottest planet, despite not being closest to the Sun.
facts.fact3: Surface pressure 92× Earth's — equivalent to being 900 m underwater.
facts.fact4: Rotates backwards; one rotation (243 Earth days) takes longer than its year (225).
facts.fact5: Atmosphere is 96.5% CO₂ with sulphuric-acid clouds — a textbook runaway greenhouse.

saturn.name: Saturn
saturn.tagline: The Solar System's signature image — a gas giant with rings.
saturn.body: Saturn is the second-largest planet in the Solar System, a ball of hydrogen and helium nine times Earth's diameter. Its rings are the largest and brightest of any planet, made almost entirely of water ice — chunks ranging from grains of sand to icebergs — orbiting in a disc only tens of metres thick. Saturn has 285 known moons, including Titan, which has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane, and Enceladus, which fires jets of water into space from a buried ocean.
saturn.narrative: Drop Saturn into a big enough bathtub and it would float. Of all the planets, it's the only one less dense than water — a gas giant so puffy that, cubic centimetre for cubic centimetre, you are denser than it is.
saturn.ifDistance: Sunlight takes 80 minutes to reach Saturn — longer than the running time of most movies. From Earth, it's 1.4 billion km on average. Every picture sent home by Cassini, which orbited Saturn for 13 years, spent well over an hour crossing that gap at the speed of light.
saturn.funFact: Saturn's rings span 282,000 km — about three-quarters of the distance from Earth to the Moon — but they're absurdly thin, often only 10 metres top to bottom. Edge-on, they almost disappear.

image.alt: Saturn with its iconic ring system seen at a 25-degree tilt.

facts.fact1: Mean diameter 116,460 km — about 9× Earth's.
facts.fact2: Average density 0.69 g/cm³ — less dense than water; would float in a big enough ocean.
facts.fact3: Rings span ~282,000 km but are only tens of metres thick.
facts.fact4: 285 known moons (as of March 2026) — more than any other planet.
facts.fact5: Cloud-top temperature around -139 °C; powered partly by heat from its own contraction.

uranus.name: Uranus
uranus.tagline: An ice giant tipped on its side.
uranus.body: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun and the third-largest by diameter. Unlike Jupiter and Saturn, much of its interior is made of "ices" — water, methane, and ammonia under extreme pressure — and trace methane in its atmosphere gives it its pale blue-green colour. Most strangely, its rotation axis is tilted 98 degrees, so it spins almost on its side. Over each 84-year orbit, each pole gets about 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness.
uranus.narrative: Voyager 2 flew past Uranus in 1986 and saw a featureless ball — partly because it arrived near solstice, with one pole aimed almost straight at the Sun, and partly because Uranus is genuinely calmer than its giant siblings. We have never sent another probe.
uranus.ifDistance: Sunlight takes 2 hours 40 minutes to reach Uranus. From Earth, it's about 2.9 billion km — so far that the planet wasn't even recognised as a planet until 1781, when William Herschel spotted it through a telescope and at first mistook it for a comet.
uranus.funFact: Uranus is the only planet in the Solar System tilted on its side. Some astronomers think it happened from a massive collision early in its history — the angle locked in for billions of years.

image.alt: Uranus as a pale blue-green disc, near-featureless and tilted nearly vertically.

facts.fact1: Diameter 50,724 km — about 4× Earth's.
facts.fact2: Year lasts 84 Earth years; axial tilt is 98° — it rolls instead of spinning.
facts.fact3: Cloud-top temperature around -197 °C — coldest planetary atmosphere despite not being farthest.
facts.fact4: Has 13 known thin, dark rings — discovered only in 1977.
facts.fact5: Discovered by William Herschel in 1781 — first planet found by telescope.

neptune.name: Neptune
neptune.tagline: A storm-blue ice giant on the edge of the planetary realm.
neptune.body: Neptune is the eighth and farthest planet, an ice giant similar in composition to Uranus but with a far more dramatic atmosphere. Voyager 2 imaged supersonic winds — the fastest in the Solar System, over 2,100 km/h — and a vast oval storm called the Great Dark Spot that has since faded and reformed elsewhere. It takes 165 Earth years for Neptune to orbit the Sun once, meaning the planet has barely completed one full orbit since it was discovered in 1846.
neptune.narrative: Neptune was the first planet discovered by mathematics rather than observation: irregularities in Uranus's orbit pointed to an unseen pull. Astronomers calculated where it should be, pointed their telescope, and saw it on the first try.
neptune.ifDistance: Sunlight takes 4 hours and 10 minutes to reach Neptune. From Earth, it's 4.5 billion km — the most distant of the eight planets, and one of the loneliest worlds we have ever photographed.
neptune.funFact: Neptune's winds blow at over 2,100 km/h — faster than the speed of sound at sea level on Earth. Why a planet this cold has the system's strongest weather is still not fully understood.

image.alt: Neptune as a deep blue disc with cirrus clouds and the Great Dark Spot visible.

facts.fact1: Diameter 49,244 km — about 3.9× Earth's.
facts.fact2: Year lasts 165 Earth years; one full orbit since discovery (1846 → 2011).
facts.fact3: Winds reach 2,100 km/h — the fastest in the Solar System.
facts.fact4: Cloud-top temperature around -201 °C, but radiates more heat than it receives.
facts.fact5: Discovered in 1846 by prediction, not observation — a triumph of Newtonian gravity.

planck_length.name: Planck Length
planck_length.tagline: The scale where our best theories stop making sense.
planck_length.body: The Planck length — about 1.6 × 10⁻³⁵ metres — is built from three constants of nature: the gravitational constant G, the speed of light c and Planck's constant ħ. The number itself is exact arithmetic; what it means is not. At this scale quantum effects and gravity should both matter at once, and no tested theory can handle that combination. It is often called the smallest possible length, but that is an expectation from candidate theories of quantum gravity — nobody has measured anything remotely this small.
planck_length.narrative: If a single atom were inflated to the size of the observable universe, the Planck length would grow to about 140 metres — roughly the height of the Great Pyramid.
planck_length.funFact: Max Planck defined it in 1899 — a year before he introduced the quantum, and 16 years before Einstein's general relativity — as a unit any civilisation, even an alien one, could rebuild from nature alone. Its role as the place where gravity and quantum mechanics collide was only understood decades later.

image.alt: A foamy, flickering lattice of spacetime at the smallest conceivable scale.

facts.fact1: Value: about 1.616 × 10⁻³⁵ m.
facts.fact2: Roughly 10²⁰ times smaller than a proton.
facts.fact3: Light crosses it in one Planck time: about 5.4 × 10⁻⁴⁴ s.
facts.fact4: Probing it directly would take about 10¹⁵ times the LHC's collision energy.

higgs_boson.name: Higgs Boson
higgs_boson.tagline: The particle that proved an invisible field fills all of space.
higgs_boson.body: In July 2012, the ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN's Large Hadron Collider announced a new particle weighing about 125 GeV — the Higgs boson, predicted back in 1964. It is a ripple in the Higgs field, which pervades the entire universe and gives elementary particles such as electrons and quarks their mass. Without it, electrons would be massless, and atoms as we know them could not form. A Higgs boson lives for only about 10⁻²² seconds, so it is never seen directly — only through the particles it decays into.
higgs_boson.narrative: The Higgs boson has no meaningful size — it is a brief excitation of a field that fills every cubic metre of space, including the one you're sitting in.
higgs_boson.massNarrative: A single Higgs boson weighs about as much as an entire caesium atom — 55 protons, 78 neutrons and 55 electrons — yet as far as anyone can tell, it has no parts inside at all.
higgs_boson.funFact: The Higgs field gives mass to electrons and quarks — yet only about 1% of your body's mass comes from it. The other 99% is energy: quarks and gluons moving and binding inside your protons and neutrons, turned into mass through E = mc².

image.alt: Particle tracks bursting from a collision point inside a detector, tracing a Higgs decay.

facts.fact1: Discovery announced at CERN on 4 July 2012.
facts.fact2: Mass: about 125 GeV — roughly 133 times a proton.
facts.fact3: Peter Higgs and François Englert shared the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physics.
facts.fact4: The LHC makes roughly one Higgs per billion proton collisions.

antimatter.name: Antimatter
antimatter.tagline: Matter's mirror twin — and the reason the universe almost shouldn't exist.
antimatter.body: Every particle has an antiparticle with the same mass but opposite charge. Paul Dirac's 1928 equation pointed to them, and in 1932 Carl Anderson spotted the first one — the positron, an anti-electron — in cosmic rays. When matter meets antimatter, both vanish in a flash of energy, exactly as E = mc² dictates. The Big Bang should have made equal amounts of each, yet everything we see is made of matter, and nobody yet knows why.
antimatter.narrative: Antimatter has no size of its own — an antiproton is exactly as big as a proton. The scale that matters is a ratio: for roughly every billion matter–antimatter pairs in the early universe, one extra particle of matter survived. That leftover is everything, including you.
antimatter.massNarrative: All the antimatter ever made at CERN, annihilated at once, would light a single light bulb for only a few minutes.
antimatter.funFact: A banana is a tiny antimatter source. Its potassium-40 very occasionally decays by emitting a positron — roughly one every hour or two — which annihilates almost instantly. Hospitals use the same physics on purpose: PET scanners image the body by catching the gamma rays from positron annihilations.

image.alt: A particle and its mirror-image antiparticle meeting in a burst of light.

facts.fact1: The positron was discovered by Carl Anderson in 1932.
facts.fact2: CERN created the first antihydrogen atoms in 1995.
facts.fact3: One gram of antimatter meeting one gram of matter releases about 1.8 × 10¹⁴ J — nearly three Hiroshima bombs.
facts.fact4: In 2023, CERN's ALPHA experiment showed antihydrogen falls down, just like matter.

quantum_entanglement.name: Quantum Entanglement
quantum_entanglement.tagline: Two particles, one shared story — however far apart they drift.
quantum_entanglement.body: When two particles become entangled, they share a single quantum state: measure one, and you instantly know what the matching measurement on the other will show, even if it is across a galaxy. Einstein found this so unsettling that he called it 'spooky action at a distance' and suspected the particles carried hidden instructions. John Bell showed in 1964 how to test that idea, and experiments since the 1970s — culminating in loophole-free tests in 2015 — say no such hidden instructions exist. Crucially, entanglement cannot send messages: each side sees perfectly random results, and the correlation only appears when the two records are compared over ordinary, light-speed-limited channels.
quantum_entanglement.narrative: Entanglement has no size of its own — it is a relationship between particles, not an object. Distance doesn't weaken it: the correlations are just as strong across a lab bench as across 1,200 km of sky.
quantum_entanglement.funFact: In a 2018 'cosmic Bell test', physicists let light from two distant quasars — emitted 7.8 and 12.2 billion years ago — decide how to measure pairs of entangled photons. Even with the settings chosen by the universe long before Earth existed, the quantum correlations held.

image.alt: Two glowing particles far apart, linked by a faint luminous thread.

facts.fact1: Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen raised the puzzle in 1935.
facts.fact2: Bell's theorem (1964) turned it into a testable prediction.
facts.fact3: 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics: Alain Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger.
facts.fact4: China's Micius satellite shared entangled photons between stations 1,203 km apart (2017).

tardigrade.name: Tardigrade
tardigrade.tagline: Half a millimetre of animal that can survive space — as long as it's dried out first.
tardigrade.body: Tardigrades, or water bears, are eight-legged micro-animals about half a millimetre long, living in moss, soil, oceans and ice on every continent. Their trick is cryptobiosis: as they dry out, they curl into a barrel-shaped 'tun', lose almost all their water and slow their metabolism to nearly zero. In that state they have endured near absolute zero, close to 150 °C for short periods, and the vacuum of space. Awake and hydrated, though, they are surprisingly fragile — a day in water at about 37 °C kills around half of one well-studied species.
tardigrade.narrative: At 0.5 mm, a tardigrade is exactly the size of Quantumaire's reference grain of sand — the size Earth shrinks to on our scale.
tardigrade.funFact: They aren't indestructible. In 2019, dried tardigrades crash-landed on the Moon aboard Israel's Beresheet lander; lab tests firing them from a gun later showed they die above about 900 m/s, so researchers think they very likely didn't survive. The confirmed revival record isn't a century, either — it is about 30 years, from Antarctic moss kept frozen since 1983.

image.alt: A plump, eight-legged tardigrade clinging to a strand of moss under the microscope.

facts.fact1: Usually up to about 0.5 mm long; the largest species reach about 1.3 mm.
facts.fact2: About 1,500 known species, first described in 1773.
facts.fact3: Can tolerate radiation doses around a thousand times what would kill a human.
facts.fact4: Dried tardigrades survived 10 days exposed to open space on FOTON-M3 in 2007.

blue_whale.name: Blue Whale
blue_whale.tagline: The largest animal known to have ever lived — built on a diet of krill.
blue_whale.body: Blue whales can reach about 30 metres and up to roughly 190 tonnes, making them the heaviest animal known to science, living or extinct. They grow that big on krill, shrimp-like crustaceans just a few centimetres long, filtered from seawater through baleen plates by the tonne. Their deep, low-frequency calls can carry for hundreds of kilometres through the ocean. Twentieth-century whaling killed hundreds of thousands of them; hunting was banned in 1966, and they are recovering only slowly.
blue_whale.narrative: A typical 25-metre adult is as long as about fifteen people lying head to toe — and a big one is longer than a basketball court.
blue_whale.massNarrative: A large blue whale outweighs about 30 elephants, and its newborn calf already weighs as much as a small elephant.
blue_whale.funFact: Its heart is huge, but not car-sized: the one preserved by Canada's Royal Ontario Museum weighs about 180 kg and stands roughly 1.5 m tall. And no, a child couldn't swim through its arteries — the aorta is only about as wide as a dinner plate.

image.alt: A blue whale gliding through sunlit open ocean, dwarfing a diver beside it.

facts.fact1: Longest reliably measured: 29.9 m.
facts.fact2: Heart: about 180 kg — the largest known in any animal.
facts.fact3: On deep dives its heart rate can drop to 2 beats per minute.
facts.fact4: Protected worldwide since 1966, but still listed as Endangered.

mount_everest.name: Mount Everest
mount_everest.tagline: The highest point above sea level — but not the tallest mountain, nor the closest to the stars.
mount_everest.body: Mount Everest rises 8,848.86 metres above sea level, a figure fixed by a joint China–Nepal survey in 2020. It exists because India has been ploughing into Asia for some 50 million years, crumpling the crust into the Himalaya — and it is still rising by roughly 2 mm a year. Measured from base to peak, Hawaii's Mauna Kea is taller, at over 10,000 m, most of it underwater. And because Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Ecuador's Chimborazo sits about 2 km farther from Earth's centre than Everest's.
mount_everest.narrative: Shrink Earth to a 30 cm desk globe and Everest becomes a bump just 0.2 mm high — about the thickness of two sheets of paper.
mount_everest.funFact: The rock at the very top of the world is marine limestone, packed with fragments of trilobites, crinoids and other sea creatures that lived on an ocean floor around 450 million years ago.

image.alt: The snow-plumed summit pyramid of Mount Everest against a deep blue high-altitude sky.

facts.fact1: Height: 8,848.86 m (China–Nepal survey, 2020).
facts.fact2: First summited on 29 May 1953 by Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary.
facts.fact3: Air pressure at the summit is only about a third of that at sea level.
facts.fact4: Average summit temperature in January: around −36 °C.

gravity.name: Gravity
gravity.tagline: The weakest force in nature — and the one that builds the cosmos.
gravity.body: Between two protons, gravity is about 10³⁶ times weaker than the electric force. Yet it never cancels out and reaches across any distance, so at large scales it wins: it rounds planets, ignites stars and herds galaxies into clusters. Newton described it in 1687 as a force between masses; Einstein's general relativity (1915) recast it as the curvature of spacetime itself. What gravity looks like at the quantum level is still unknown — its proposed particle, the graviton, has never been detected.
gravity.narrative: Gravity has no size of its own: its reach is unlimited, fading with the square of distance but never quite reaching zero. The same pull that keeps your feet on the floor shapes structures hundreds of millions of light-years across.
gravity.funFact: A small fridge magnet can lift a paperclip off the table — out-pulling the gravity of the entire Earth, all 6 × 10²⁴ kg of it. That's how feeble gravity is, until you gather a planet's worth of mass.

image.alt: A grid of spacetime curving into a deep well around a massive glowing sphere.

facts.fact1: About 10³⁶ times weaker than electromagnetism between two protons.
facts.fact2: Surface gravity on Earth: about 9.81 m/s².
facts.fact3: Newton's law of gravitation: 1687; Einstein's general relativity: 1915.
facts.fact4: No confirmed quantum theory of gravity — the graviton remains hypothetical.

time_dilation.name: Time Dilation
time_dilation.tagline: Time runs at different speeds — and your phone has to correct for it.
time_dilation.body: Relativity says there is no universal clock. A clock that moves fast runs slow (special relativity), and a clock deep in a gravity well runs slow too (general relativity). The effect has been measured again and again: in 1971 Hafele and Keating flew atomic clocks around the world on airliners and saw them disagree by hundreds of nanoseconds. Muons created high in the atmosphere should decay long before reaching the ground — yet they arrive in large numbers, because their clocks tick slowly at nearly the speed of light.
time_dilation.narrative: Time dilation has no size — it's a difference in the rate of time itself. It is measurable across a whole planet's orbit and, with today's best atomic clocks, across a height difference of a few centimetres.
time_dilation.funFact: GPS satellites' clocks gain about 38 microseconds a day relative to the ground — losing 7 to their speed but gaining 45 from weaker gravity. Uncorrected, your position fix would drift by roughly 10 km every day.

image.alt: Two clocks ticking at different rates, one near Earth and one in orbit, against curved spacetime.
